newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire peace parley scrapped, spotlight on Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Zaire peace parley scrapped, spotlight on Kinshasa.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela has failed to bring Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila together for crunch peace talks, raising the likelihood of a battle for the capital Kinshasa.

U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said Mandela abruptly called off Wednesday's planned ship-borne talks in response to a last-minute demand by Kabila that they be held in international waters and not in Congo's port of Pointe Noire.
But a senior South African official said Kabila, whose forces have been advancing on Kinshasa, had agreed to meet Mandela in South Africa on Thursday.
"He has indicated that he is committed to continuing the talks," Frank Chikane, an aide to Mandela's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, said on the South African ice-breaker Outeniqua.
Mandela left for South Africa after talks with Mobutu, who suffers from cancer and reportedly had to be roused from bed to meet him.

Sahnoun said he and Mandela, who has been trying to broker a peaceful transfer of power, had not abandoned hope. "We are not going to give up. We will continue to try to avoid another humanitarian tragedy," he said.
Rebel spokesmen said Kabila, 56, whose forces now control three-quarters of Africa's third largest nation, had insisted on talks at sea on security grounds.
Mobutu's government in Kinshasa said it remained ready to give peace talks a chance but it was not immediately clear if, or when, the veteran Zairean leader would return home.
"We do not think that the dialogue has broken down," government spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba said in Kinshasa, adding that Mobutu would probably not return on Wednesday.

The capital itself, largely shut down on Wednesday by an opposition stay-home protest against Mobutu, began its second night under curfew in the seven-month-old war. Troops have orders to shoot looters.
Mobutu, 66, who has reputedly amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, have made lightning advances across the impoverished, corruption-plagued nation.

Mobutu agreed at peace talks on May 4 to hand power to an elected president. Kabila, both then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Rebel radio suggested Kabila's forces were nearing the approaches to Kinshasa. The government dismissed such reports.
Kin-Kiey, who is also information minister, said the war front had stabilised some 200 km (120 miles) east of the capital and government troops were fighting with "courage and determination".

Rebel Justice "Commissioner-General" Mwenze Kongolo said by telephone from Angola's Cabinda enclave, where Kabila was waiting to join the talks, that the rebels were advancing on Kinshasa. "Military activities continue as usual," he said.
The United States said it was "very disappointed" that Wednesday's planned talks had fallen through.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns urged Kabila and Mobutu to speak to each other, "or else we fear for future events".
